title: The Treasury Secretary Trades the Bond Market Like a Position — and Prices Will Win
dek: US Treasury Secretary Bessent is intervening in the bond market, trade, and sanctions with a trader's mindset, but inflation and deficits keep prices rising, making his strategy likely to fail.
why: A deep dive into Bessent's multi-front interventions and their internal contradictions, offering unique insight into US fiscal policy and market dynamics.
who: Investors, policy analysts, and financial journalists focused on US fiscal policy, the Treasury market, and macroeconomic dynamics.
skip: The opening review of Bessent's career can be skipped; go straight to the intervention details.

points.h: The Treasury Secretary Treats Debt Management Like a Trading Position
points.body: Bessent treats Treasury management as a trading position rather than a neutral operation. He believes the market is mispricing the 10-year yield and is betting that long-term rates will fall. To that end, he is buying back long-dated bonds and issuing short-dated ones to shorten the debt's duration and push down long-term yields. If he is right, the government can refinance at lower rates; if wrong, it must keep rolling over short-term debt at market rates, with huge risk.

points.h: Suppressing Yields Is Turning Off the Deficit Alarm
points.body: Druckenmiller wrote in the Wall Street Journal that Bessent's buybacks are not liquidity management but an attempt to change a number the government dislikes. He notes there is no sign of market dysfunction; rising yields are a true reflection of inflation, deficits, and debt. Suppressing yields is like turning off the alarm that forces politicians to address deficits — every basis point is a subsidy for delay.

points.h: Bond Yields Are Arithmetic; Armies Can't Conquer Them
points.body: Trump hinted at using military means to solve high interest rates, and when asked whether he had directed intervention in the bond market, Bessent did not deny it. Boyle jokes that he doesn't know how the military would intervene in bond yields, but notes that when all economic tools fail, the military becomes the last option. Yet yields are an arithmetic result; they cannot be invaded or blockaded.

points.h: Tariff Wars and Lower Long-Term Yields Can't Succeed Simultaneously
points.body: Tariffs on Canada are ultimately borne by US consumers, raising production costs and prices. Higher inflation leads bond investors to demand higher yields, working against Bessent's efforts to push down long-term rates. The trade war and bond market intervention contradict each other, like stepping on the gas and pulling the handbrake at the same time.

points.h: Without Sanctioning China, Pressure on Iran Is Empty Talk
points.body: Bessent previewed an 'economic D-Day' for Iran, but the final result was sanctions on only about 60 entities, with no country or deadline named. Since China buys about 90% of Iran's crude oil, real pressure would require sanctioning China, but Trump is about to meet Xi Jinping, making that politically unworkable. Iranian negotiators openly mocked the US bluff.

points.h: Stablecoins Are Both a Sanctions Loophole and a Buyer of Short-Dated Debt
points.body: The government sanctions Iran on one hand, yet promotes cryptocurrencies on the other, and Iran is using crypto to evade sanctions. Bessent expects the stablecoin market to grow to $2 trillion, creating demand for short-term Treasuries to support his buyback strategy. This creates the awkward situation of relying on a channel used by the enemy.

points.h: Warsh Hints at Rate Hikes, the Opposite of the Treasury Secretary's Bet
points.body: New Fed Chair Warsh said at Jackson Hole that inflation has exceeded the target for 65 consecutive months and that financial conditions are not restrictive, hinting at possible rate hikes. Market expectations for a September hike rose from 35% to 60%. Warsh and Bessent are at odds: one sees high yields as a problem, the other as a signal.

points.h: A Third of Treasuries Mature Within a Year — That's a Bet on Rate Cuts
points.body: About a third of marketable Treasuries mature within 12 months; financing with short-term bills is a bet that rates will fall. If Warsh hikes, the maturity wall will push interest costs higher. Bessent's '333' plan (deficit to 3% of GDP, growth at 3%, energy production up 3%) has already gone off track, with growth at 1.5%-2% and the deficit about twice the target.
